brief: Friday's VIX and VVIX spike showed forced deleveraging, risk managers cutting exposure and traders paying up for tail protection: panic hedging, not ordinary volatility buying. Tail gauges SDEX and TDEX moved even more than VIX itself. GS's Lee Coppersmith called Friday the first real sign of panic in index hedging, after weeks of damage beneath the surface. Hedging demand hit record levels: VIX futures volume reached 3.6x its 20-day average, Cboe index put volume hit an all-time high, total put volume was the fourth-highest since 2015, and VIX call volume was the second-highest in five years, behind only August 2, 2024, days before VIX spiked above 60. Relative to the SPX's decline, the VIX move was an outlier: since 1990 only nine sessions saw a larger VIX spike alongside a smaller SPX drop. The note also flags that equity volatility had stayed complacent against building credit stress (CDX IG). Friday broke that complacency, but the gap remains wide. Dealer gamma fell $5.9bn, pushing aggregate positioning toward neutral and risking a spread of volatility from single stocks to the index. The note calls this extreme fear, short of April's panic, and asks whether buying it, historically profitable, works this time.
